lessons.title: The Origins of the Weimar Republic 1918–19
lessons.description: Germany's defeat, the Kaiser's abdication, and the new Weimar Constitution.
lessons.content_html:
Germany at the End of the First World War

By autumn 1918, Germany was losing the war. The British naval blockade had caused widespread food shortages — an estimated 750,000 German civilians died from starvation and related diseases during the war. Soldiers were exhausted after four years of fighting, morale had collapsed, and the German army was in retreat on the Western Front. The entry of the United States into the war in 1917 had tipped the balance decisively against Germany.

On the home front, conditions were desperate. The winter of 1917–18 became known as the “Turnip Winter” because turnips were one of the few foods still available. Fuel was scarce, and many Germans blamed the Kaiser and the military leadership for continuing a war that could not be won.

Key Fact

By October 1918, Germany faced military defeat, mass starvation from the British blockade, and collapsing morale among both soldiers and civilians. These combined pressures made political change inevitable.

Political Unrest and Revolution

In late October 1918, German sailors at Kiel mutinied, refusing to sail out for a final battle against the British Royal Navy. The mutiny spread rapidly. Workers and soldiers across Germany formed councils (similar to the Russian soviets) and took control of cities including Hamburg, Bremen, and Munich. By early November, a full-scale revolution was under way.

On 29 October 1918, naval commanders ordered the German fleet to sail from Kiel for a final attack on the British navy. Sailors saw this as a suicide mission and refused to obey. When the authorities arrested around 1,000 sailors, their comrades rose up in protest. Within days, 40,000 sailors had joined the revolt. The mutiny triggered uprisings across Germany as workers and soldiers demanded peace and political change.

The Abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II

Kaiser Wilhelm II had ruled Germany as an autocratic monarch since 1888. As revolution spread, his position became impossible. On 9 November 1918, Chancellor Max von Baden announced the Kaiser’s abdication without the Kaiser’s permission. Wilhelm fled to the Netherlands, where he lived in exile until his death in 1941. Germany’s monarchy was over.

Key Fact

Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November 1918. His abdication was announced by Chancellor Max von Baden before the Kaiser had actually agreed, showing the urgency of the political crisis.

The Armistice

On 11 November 1918, the new government signed an armistice with the Allies, bringing the fighting to an end. The armistice required Germany to withdraw its troops from occupied territories, surrender its navy and heavy weapons, and allow Allied forces to occupy the Rhineland. Many Germans felt humiliated by these terms, but the country had no choice — continuing the war was impossible.

29 Oct 1918

Kiel Mutiny Begins

Sailors refuse to sail for a final battle against Britain.

9 Nov 1918

Kaiser Abdicates

Wilhelm II’s abdication is announced; he flees to the Netherlands.

11 Nov 1918

Armistice Signed

Fighting ends at 11am. Germany surrenders its fleet and heavy weapons.

The New Republic

On 9 November 1918, Friedrich Ebert, leader of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), became Germany’s new leader. In January 1919, elections were held for a National Assembly, which met in the city of Weimar (Berlin was too dangerous due to ongoing street fighting). Ebert was elected as the first President of the new republic. The assembly’s main task was to create a new democratic constitution for Germany.

The National Assembly met in Weimar rather than Berlin because the capital was gripped by political violence. Communist revolutionaries (the Spartacists) were fighting government forces in the streets. Weimar was a smaller, safer city with strong cultural associations — it was the home of Goethe and Schiller, great German writers, which gave the new republic a sense of intellectual respectability.

The Weimar Constitution: Strengths and Weaknesses

The new constitution was one of the most democratic in the world. All men and women over 20 could vote. The Reichstag (parliament) was elected using proportional representation, and a Bill of Rights guaranteed freedoms of speech, religion, and equality before the law.

Key Fact

The Weimar Constitution had key strengths (universal suffrage, Bill of Rights, elected parliament) but also critical weaknesses: proportional representation led to unstable coalition governments, and Article 48 allowed the President to rule by decree in an emergency — a power that could be dangerously abused.

Strengths: Universal suffrage for men and women over 20. A Bill of Rights protected individual freedoms. The President was directly elected by the people. The Reichstag had the power to pass laws, and the government was accountable to it. Germany’s 18 regions (Länder) kept local powers.

Weaknesses: Proportional representation meant small parties won seats easily, making it almost impossible for one party to gain a majority. This led to weak coalition governments that often disagreed and collapsed. Article 48 allowed the President to suspend the Reichstag and pass laws by decree in an “emergency” — but the constitution did not clearly define what counted as an emergency, leaving this open to abuse.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Germany’s military defeat, the naval blockade, and collapsing morale led to revolution in November 1918, forcing the Kaiser to abdicate and the armistice to be signed.
  • The Weimar Republic was established in 1919 with a democratic constitution, but proportional representation created weak coalition governments, and Article 48 gave the President dangerous emergency powers.
  • The republic was born out of defeat and revolution, meaning it faced hostility from both the political left and right from the very beginning.

lessons.title: Early Challenges: Versailles, Spartacists & the Kapp Putsch
lessons.description: The Treaty of Versailles, the 'stab in the back' myth, and violent uprisings from left and right.
lessons.content_html:
The Treaty of Versailles (1919)

In June 1919, Germany was forced to sign the Treaty of Versailles. The German government had no choice — the Allies threatened to resume the war if Germany refused. The treaty was a diktat (dictated peace) because Germany was not allowed to negotiate the terms. Germans across the political spectrum were outraged.

Key Fact

The key terms of the Treaty of Versailles can be remembered as LAMB: Land — Germany lost 13% of its territory including Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Corridor, and all overseas colonies. Army — limited to 100,000 men, no air force, only 6 battleships, no submarines, no tanks. Money — reparations set at £6.6 billion in 1921. Blame — Article 231 (the War Guilt Clause) forced Germany to accept full responsibility for starting the war.

Germany lost approximately 13% of its European territory and 10% of its population. Key losses included: Alsace-Lorraine returned to France; the Polish Corridor and Upper Silesia given to Poland, splitting East Prussia from the rest of Germany; the Saar coalfields placed under League of Nations control for 15 years; Danzig made a free city; the Rhineland demilitarised (no German troops allowed). All overseas colonies were taken away and given to the Allies as “mandates.” These losses stripped Germany of valuable farmland, industrial resources, and a significant chunk of its population.

Why Was the Treaty So Unpopular?

Germans were furious for several reasons. They felt the treaty was unjust because Germany had not been allowed to negotiate. The War Guilt Clause (Article 231) was particularly hated — most Germans did not believe they alone had started the war. The massive reparations bill threatened to cripple the economy. The military restrictions humiliated a proud nation. And the loss of territory separated millions of German-speaking people from their homeland.

The politicians who signed the treaty became known as the “November Criminals” — they were blamed for surrendering when many Germans believed the army had never actually been defeated on the battlefield.

The “Stab in the Back” Theory

The Dolchstoßlegende (“stab in the back” myth) claimed that the German army had not been defeated in the field but had been betrayed by politicians, socialists, and Jews on the home front. This was a lie — Germany’s military position was hopeless by November 1918 — but it was widely believed, especially by right-wing nationalists. The myth was devastating for the Weimar Republic because it linked the new democratic government with betrayal and humiliation. Hitler later used it extensively in Nazi propaganda.

Key Fact

The “stab in the back” theory was a myth, but it fatally damaged the Weimar Republic by associating the new democratic government with defeat and betrayal. Right-wing groups used it to attack the Republic throughout the 1920s.

The Spartacist Uprising (January 1919)

Not everyone wanted a democratic republic. The Spartacists were a communist group led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. They wanted a workers’ revolution like the one in Russia. In January 1919, they launched an uprising in Berlin, seizing key buildings including newspaper offices.

President Ebert used the Freikorps — right-wing ex-soldiers — to crush the revolt. The Freikorps brutally suppressed the Spartacists within days. Luxemburg and Liebknecht were captured and murdered on 15 January 1919. The uprising failed, but Ebert’s reliance on the Freikorps showed the government’s weakness — it could not even use its own army to maintain order.

The Freikorps were groups of demobilised soldiers who refused to give up their weapons after the war. They were fiercely nationalist, anti-communist, and often violent. The Weimar government used them because the regular army (limited to 100,000 by the Treaty of Versailles) was too small to deal with uprisings. This was a dangerous bargain — the Freikorps despised the Republic almost as much as they despised communism.

The Kapp Putsch (March 1920)

The threat came from the political right too. In March 1920, Dr Wolfgang Kapp and a group of Freikorps soldiers marched into Berlin and seized control of the government. The regular army refused to fire on the Freikorps — “troops do not fire on troops,” declared General von Seeckt. The government fled to Stuttgart.

The putsch was defeated not by the army but by the workers of Berlin, who launched a general strike. With no electricity, water, gas, or transport, Kapp could not govern. The putsch collapsed after just four days. However, the episode revealed two alarming facts: the army could not be relied upon to defend the Republic, and right-wing extremism was a serious threat.

Key Fact

The Spartacist uprising (left-wing, January 1919) was crushed by the Freikorps. The Kapp Putsch (right-wing, March 1920) was defeated by a general strike. Both showed the Weimar Republic was vulnerable to extremists on both sides of the political spectrum.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Edexcel Paper 3 “Explain why” questions (8 marks), you should aim for three developed points. Each point needs specific knowledge (names, dates, figures) linked with explanation words like “this meant that” or “as a result.” If the question gives you stimulus points, use them — but you must also include your own knowledge beyond what’s suggested.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Treaty of Versailles (LAMB: Land, Army, Money, Blame) was hated by Germans and fatally linked the Weimar Republic with humiliation and defeat.
  • The “stab in the back” myth falsely claimed the army was undefeated, undermining the Republic’s legitimacy from the start.
  • Violent challenges from the left (Spartacists) and right (Kapp Putsch) showed the Republic was fragile and could not rely on its own army for protection.

lessons.title: Crisis of 1923: Hyperinflation & the Ruhr
lessons.description: Why France invaded the Ruhr, how hyperinflation destroyed savings, and its impact on German society.
lessons.content_html:
The French Occupation of the Ruhr

In January 1923, Germany fell behind on its reparations payments. France and Belgium responded by sending troops into the Ruhr — Germany’s industrial heartland — to seize goods, raw materials, and factory output as payment. The French argued they were entitled to take what Germany owed by force.

The German government under Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno called for passive resistance — workers in the Ruhr were told to stop working and refuse to cooperate with the French. The government promised to continue paying their wages. This policy was popular because it united Germans against a common enemy, but it was economically catastrophic.

Key Fact

France invaded the Ruhr in January 1923 because Germany missed reparations payments. The German government called for passive resistance, but paying idle workers while receiving no industrial output forced the government to print more and more money — triggering hyperinflation.

The occupation was humiliating and violent. French troops killed over 130 Germans during the occupation, including workers shot during protests. Around 150,000 Germans were expelled from their homes in the Ruhr. Factories and mines were seized. The loss of the Ruhr’s industrial output was devastating — the region produced about 80% of Germany’s coal, iron, and steel. Without this output, the German economy ground to a halt.

The Causes of Hyperinflation

Hyperinflation did not happen overnight. Its roots lay in the war. Between 1914 and 1918, the German government had borrowed heavily and printed money to fund the war effort rather than raising taxes. By the end of the war, the amount of money in circulation had increased massively but the amount of goods available had not — so prices rose.

The Treaty of Versailles made things worse. Reparations payments drained the economy. When the Ruhr was occupied in 1923 and the government called for passive resistance, it had to pay the wages of millions of idle workers. The only way to do this was to print even more money. The result was a catastrophic spiral: more money in circulation meant each banknote was worth less, so prices rose even further, so the government printed even more money.

The Scale of Hyperinflation

The numbers were staggering. In January 1921, a loaf of bread cost 0.63 marks. By January 1923, it cost 250 marks. By September 1923, it cost 1.5 million marks. By November 1923, a single loaf cost an almost incomprehensible 200 billion marks. Workers were paid twice a day and rushed to spend their wages before prices rose again. People carried cash in wheelbarrows and used banknotes as wallpaper because the paper was worth more than the printed value.

Key Fact

The price of a loaf of bread rose from 0.63 marks in January 1921 to 200 billion marks by November 1923. German currency became effectively worthless within months.

Winners and Losers of Hyperinflation

Hyperinflation did not affect everyone equally. Understanding who gained and who lost is essential for exam questions about the impact on German society.

Savers were devastated. People who had carefully saved money their entire lives found their savings were now worthless. A life’s savings might not buy a cup of coffee. The middle classes (Mittelstand) were hit hardest — they had savings, fixed incomes, and pensions that lost all value. Pensioners and those on fixed incomes suffered terribly because their payments stayed the same while prices rocketed. Wage earners struggled because, even when wages were adjusted, they could never keep pace with rising prices.

People with debts benefited because they could repay loans in worthless currency. A mortgage that would have taken years to pay off could be settled for the price of a loaf of bread. Businesspeople and industrialists who owned physical assets (factories, land, goods) saw those assets hold their value while debts melted away. Foreign visitors with hard currency could buy German goods and property at rock-bottom prices. Some shrewd speculators made fortunes.

The Impact on German Society

The social consequences of hyperinflation were profound. The middle classes — the backbone of any stable democracy — felt betrayed by the Republic. Many had supported the war, saved responsibly, and played by the rules, only to lose everything. Their bitterness and resentment made them receptive to extremist political movements in the years that followed.

Crime and social breakdown increased. Food riots broke out in cities. Theft became common as people struggled to feed their families. There was a widespread feeling that the Weimar government was incompetent and unable to protect its citizens. This loss of faith in democratic government would have lasting consequences.

Key Fact

Hyperinflation destroyed middle-class savings and faith in the Weimar Republic. The bitterness this created among the Mittelstand was a key reason many later turned to extremist parties, including the Nazis, in the early 1930s.

lessons.title: Stresemann & the Golden Age 1924–29
lessons.description: Economic recovery, international diplomacy, and cultural change during Weimar's 'Golden Years'.
lessons.content_html:
Stresemann and Economic Recovery

Gustav Stresemann became Chancellor in August 1923, at the height of the hyperinflation crisis. Although he was Chancellor for only 100 days, he then served as Foreign Minister until his death in 1929. His actions during these years are often credited with saving the Weimar Republic — at least temporarily.

Stresemann’s first priority was to end hyperinflation. He called off passive resistance in the Ruhr (an unpopular decision that angered nationalists) and introduced a new currency, the Rentenmark, in November 1923. The Rentenmark was backed by German land and industrial assets rather than gold, and it was issued in strictly limited quantities. Confidence in the currency was restored remarkably quickly.

Key Fact

Stresemann introduced the Rentenmark in November 1923 to end hyperinflation. This was followed by the Dawes Plan (1924) and the Young Plan (1929), which restructured reparations and brought American investment flooding into Germany.

The Dawes Plan (1924)

In 1924, the Dawes Plan, negotiated with the United States, restructured Germany’s reparations. Annual payments were reduced and linked to Germany’s ability to pay. Crucially, American banks loaned $800 million to Germany to help rebuild its economy. French and Belgian troops withdrew from the Ruhr.

American money poured into Germany. Factories were modernised, new roads and public buildings were constructed, and employment rose. Between 1924 and 1929, Germany received around $3 billion in loans and investment from the United States. The economy appeared to be booming.

In 1929, the Young Plan further reduced the total reparations bill from £6.6 billion to approximately £2 billion and extended the payment period to 59 years (until 1988). This eased the burden on Germany, but right-wing nationalists — including Hitler — attacked it, arguing that Germany should not be paying reparations at all.

International Acceptance: Locarno and the League

Stresemann’s greatest achievements were in foreign policy. In 1925, Germany signed the Locarno Pact, voluntarily accepting its western borders with France and Belgium as set by the Treaty of Versailles. This was significant because Germany was choosing to cooperate rather than being forced — it marked a shift from resentment to reconciliation.

In 1926, Germany was admitted to the League of Nations, taking a permanent seat on the Council alongside Britain, France, Italy, and Japan. This was a powerful symbol: Germany was being welcomed back into the international community after the humiliation of Versailles. Stresemann won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 for his work at Locarno.

Key Fact

The Locarno Pact (1925) and League of Nations membership (1926) restored Germany’s international standing. However, Germany only accepted its western borders — it did not accept its eastern borders with Poland, leaving future conflict possible.

Was It Really a “Golden Age”?

The recovery had serious weaknesses. Germany’s prosperity depended almost entirely on American loans. If the loans were recalled, the economy would collapse — which is exactly what happened after the Wall Street Crash of 1929. Unemployment never fell below 1 million during the “Golden Years.” Farmers suffered from falling food prices throughout the period. Many middle-class Germans had not recovered from the hyperinflation of 1923 and remained bitter.

Strengths: Industrial output recovered and surpassed pre-war levels by 1928. Exports rose. New housing was built. Wages increased for many workers. Germany was readmitted to the international community.

Weaknesses: Dependence on American loans made recovery fragile. Unemployment stayed above 1 million. Farmers struggled with low prices. Extremist parties (Nazis and Communists) still won seats in the Reichstag. The middle classes had not recovered their savings from hyperinflation. 28 coalition governments in 14 years showed ongoing political instability.

Changes in Society and Culture

The Weimar period saw dramatic social and cultural changes, especially in cities like Berlin. Women gained new freedoms: they could vote, enter professions, and enjoyed greater social independence. Some women cut their hair short, wore more daring fashions, and smoked in public — the image of the “New Woman.” By 1925, 36% of the German workforce was female.

Culturally, Germany became a centre of innovation. The Bauhaus school, founded by Walter Gropius in 1919, revolutionised architecture and design with its clean, functional style. Expressionist art flourished, with artists like Otto Dix and George Grosz producing powerful (and often controversial) work. The German film industry thrived — Fritz Lang’s Metropolis (1927) became one of the most influential films ever made. Cabaret culture in Berlin pushed social boundaries.

Not everyone welcomed these changes. Many conservative and rural Germans saw the new culture as immoral and decadent. The Nazis later called Weimar art “degenerate” and blamed it on Jewish influence. The gap between progressive urban culture and traditional rural values deepened political divisions. For many older and more conservative Germans, the cultural changes of the 1920s were another reason to distrust the Republic.

Key Fact

The “Golden Years” saw significant cultural innovation (Bauhaus, expressionist art, cinema) and changes in women’s roles, but these changes divided opinion — conservatives saw them as evidence of moral decline, deepening the political divide.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark “How far do you agree?” question, you need to argue both sides. A common question on this topic is whether the period 1924–29 was truly a “Golden Age.” Make sure you balance evidence of recovery (Rentenmark, Dawes Plan, Locarno, cultural achievements) against evidence of continuing problems (American loan dependence, unemployment, middle-class bitterness, political instability). End with a clear, supported judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stresemann stabilised the economy with the Rentenmark, the Dawes Plan, and the Young Plan, and restored Germany’s international standing through the Locarno Pact and League of Nations membership.
  • The recovery was fragile — it depended on American loans, unemployment stayed high, farmers struggled, and the middle classes had not recovered from hyperinflation.
  • Cultural changes (Bauhaus, expressionism, the “New Woman”) were celebrated by progressives but condemned by conservatives, deepening political divisions that extremists would later exploit.

lessons.title: Hitler’s Early Career & the Munich Putsch 1923
lessons.description: Hitler's rise through the Nazi Party, the failed Munich Putsch, and Mein Kampf's lasting impact.
lessons.content_html:
Hitler Joins the German Workers’ Party

Adolf Hitler was born in Austria in 1889. He served as a corporal in the German army during the First World War and was devastated by Germany’s defeat. Like many right-wing nationalists, he believed the stab in the back myth and blamed socialists and Jews for Germany’s surrender.

In September 1919, the army sent Hitler to spy on a small political group called the German Workers’ Party (DAP), founded by Anton Drexler in Munich. Instead of reporting back, Hitler was drawn to the party’s nationalist and anti-Semitic ideas. He joined as member number 555 (though the party started numbering at 500 to appear larger). Hitler quickly became the party’s most effective speaker, drawing in new members with his passionate, angry style of oratory.

Key Fact

Hitler joined the German Workers’ Party (DAP) in September 1919. By February 1920, the party had been renamed the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP) — the Nazi Party — and had announced its Twenty-Five Point Programme.

The Twenty-Five Point Programme

In February 1920, Hitler and Drexler published the Twenty-Five Point Programme, the party’s political manifesto. Its key demands included: the abolition of the Treaty of Versailles; the unification of all German-speaking people into a “Greater Germany”; citizenship only for those of “German blood” (explicitly excluding Jews); land reform and the nationalisation of large businesses; and a strong central government.

The programme appealed to a wide range of discontented Germans. Nationalists supported the rejection of Versailles. Workers liked the promises of nationalisation and land reform. Anti-Semites approved of the exclusion of Jews. The combination of nationalism and socialism in the party name was deliberately designed to attract support from across the political spectrum.

Point 1: Union of all Germans in a Greater Germany. Point 2: Abolition of the Treaty of Versailles. Point 4: Only those of “German blood” can be citizens; no Jew can be a citizen. Point 7: Non-citizens to be expelled if the state cannot feed its people. Point 13: Nationalisation of large businesses. Point 17: Land reform for the common good. Point 25: A strong central authority for the Reich. These demands combined extreme nationalism with populist economic promises.

The Role of the SA

In 1921, Hitler became leader of the Nazi Party. He established the SA (Sturmabteilung, or Storm Section), a paramilitary force also known as the “Brownshirts.” The SA’s role was to protect Nazi meetings, disrupt the meetings of rival parties, and intimidate opponents. Many SA members were ex-soldiers and Freikorps men who were attracted by the violence and discipline. The SA gave the Nazi Party a visible, aggressive presence on the streets that other parties could not match.

The Munich Putsch (8–9 November 1923)

By late 1923, Hitler believed the time was right to seize power. Germany was in crisis: hyperinflation was destroying the economy, the French occupied the Ruhr, and the government appeared weak. Hitler was inspired by Mussolini’s March on Rome in 1922, which had brought the fascists to power in Italy. He planned to seize control of Munich first, then march on Berlin.

8 Nov 1923

The Beer Hall

Hitler and 600 SA men stormed a beer hall in Munich where Bavarian leaders were meeting. At gunpoint, Hitler forced Gustav von Kahr (head of the Bavarian government), General von Lossow, and Colonel von Seisser to support his plan to overthrow the national government.

9 Nov 1923

The March

The next morning, around 2,000 Nazis marched through Munich towards the War Ministry. However, Kahr and Lossow had alerted the police and army. Armed police blocked the marchers at the Feldherrnhalle. Shots were fired; 16 Nazis and 4 police officers were killed. Hitler dislocated his shoulder and fled, but was arrested two days later.

Key Fact

The Munich Putsch failed militarily — 16 Nazis were killed and Hitler was arrested. But the consequences transformed the Nazi movement: Hitler’s trial gave him a national platform, prison gave him time to write Mein Kampf, and he concluded that power must be seized through legal, democratic means.

Consequences of the Munich Putsch

Hitler was put on trial for treason in February 1924. He used the trial as propaganda, making passionate speeches that were reported across Germany. The sympathetic judges gave him the minimum sentence of five years, and he served only nine months in the comfortable Landsberg Prison.

While in prison, Hitler dictated Mein Kampf (“My Struggle”) to his deputy, Rudolf Hess. The book set out Hitler’s core beliefs: extreme racial ideology (Aryan supremacy and violent anti-Semitism), Lebensraum (living space — the idea that Germany needed to expand eastward into Poland and Russia), hatred of communism, and the Führerprinzip (the belief that Germany needed one all-powerful leader). Although poorly written and rambling, Mein Kampf sold over 5 million copies by 1939 and became the ideological foundation of the Nazi state.

Rebuilding the Party: The Bamberg Conference (1926)

After his release from prison in December 1924, Hitler set about rebuilding the Nazi Party along new lines. He recognised that the Munich Putsch had proved that violent revolution would not work in Germany — the army and police would simply crush it. Instead, he adopted a strategy of gaining power through legal means — winning elections and then using democratic institutions to destroy democracy from within.

At the Bamberg Conference in February 1926, Hitler reasserted his personal authority over the party. Some members, led by Gregor Strasser in northern Germany, wanted the party to focus more on socialist policies to attract workers. Hitler crushed this opposition, establishing the Führerprinzip — the principle that the leader’s word was absolute and final. The party was reorganised into regional districts (Gaue) to fight elections across Germany.

Key Fact

The Bamberg Conference (1926) established two crucial principles: Hitler’s absolute authority over the party (Führerprinzip) and the strategy of gaining power through elections rather than armed revolt. These decisions shaped the Nazi Party’s path to power.

Despite Hitler’s reorganisation, the Nazis remained a fringe party during the “Golden Years.” In the 1928 Reichstag elections, the Nazis won only 12 seats and 2.6% of the vote. Stresemann’s economic recovery meant most Germans were reasonably content — they had no reason to vote for an extremist party. The Nazis’ message of anger and national humiliation had less appeal when the economy was growing and Germany was being accepted back into the international community.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hitler joined the DAP in 1919, renamed it the Nazi Party in 1920, and published the Twenty-Five Point Programme combining extreme nationalism with anti-Semitism and populist economic promises.
  • The Munich Putsch (November 1923) failed as a seizure of power, but its consequences — national publicity, Mein Kampf, and a shift to legal strategy — were crucial to the Nazis’ long-term rise.
  • The Bamberg Conference (1926) established Hitler’s absolute authority and the strategy of winning power through elections, though the Nazis remained a fringe party during the prosperous mid-1920s.

lessons.title: The Growth of Nazi Support 1929–32
lessons.description: How economic crisis and clever propaganda turned the Nazis from a fringe party into a mass movement.
lessons.content_html:
The Wall Street Crash and Its Impact on Germany

In October 1929, the Wall Street Crash sent shockwaves across the world. Share prices on the New York stock exchange collapsed, and American banks demanded the repayment of their loans to Germany. Under the Dawes Plan, Germany had borrowed heavily from the USA to fund its economic recovery during the 1920s. When this money was recalled, German businesses closed, banks failed, and unemployment soared.

Key Fact

By January 1932, unemployment in Germany had reached over 6 million — roughly one in three of the workforce. Millions more were on short-time working or reduced wages.

The Weimar government struggled to respond. Chancellor Brüning cut government spending and raised taxes, which made the depression worse. People lost faith in democracy. Desperate and angry, many Germans turned to extremist parties that promised radical solutions — the Nazis on the far right and the Communists on the far left.

The Growth of the Communist Party

The Communist Party (KPD) grew rapidly during the Depression. By November 1932, the KPD won 100 seats in the Reichstag. The Communists drew support from the unemployed and industrial workers, promising to redistribute wealth and nationalise industry. Their growth terrified Germany’s industrialists, landowners, and middle classes, who feared a Communist revolution like the one in Russia in 1917.

The stronger the Communists became, the more frightened the middle classes and elites grew. Many wealthy industrialists began funding the Nazi Party because Hitler promised to crush communism. Ordinary middle-class Germans also turned to the Nazis as a barrier against a Communist takeover. Fear of communism was one of the Nazis’ most effective recruitment tools — they positioned themselves as the only party strong enough to stop the “Red threat.”

The Appeal of Hitler and the Nazi Party

Hitler was a gifted public speaker who could whip up a crowd’s emotions. He offered simple solutions to complex problems, blaming Germany’s suffering on the Treaty of Versailles, the Weimar politicians (the “November Criminals”), and Jewish people. His message appealed to different groups for different reasons:

  • The unemployed were promised jobs through public works and rearmament.
  • The middle classes were offered protection from communism and a return to traditional values.
  • Farmers were promised higher food prices and protection from foreign imports.
  • Industrialists were promised the destruction of trade unions and Communist organisations.
  • Nationalists were promised the reversal of the Treaty of Versailles and the restoration of German greatness.
Key Fact

The Nazis’ appeal was deliberately broad. Hitler told each audience what it wanted to hear, offering something for everyone while keeping his core message of national renewal vague enough to avoid alienating potential supporters.

Goebbels and Nazi Propaganda

Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi propaganda in 1930. He was a master of mass communication and used every available medium to spread the Nazi message. Goebbels organised rallies, torchlight parades, and mass meetings that created an atmosphere of power and excitement. He pioneered the use of radio, film, and posters, and ensured that Nazi slogans like “Work and Bread” were plastered across Germany.

Hitler himself flew across Germany by aeroplane during election campaigns — the “Hitler over Germany” tour of 1932 saw him visit 20 cities in just seven days. This was revolutionary for the time and helped create the image of a dynamic, modern leader who was everywhere at once.

Mass rallies — huge, carefully staged events with banners, music, and marching that made the Nazis look powerful and disciplined. Posters and leaflets — simple, bold messages targeting specific groups (workers, farmers, women). Radio — Goebbels recognised radio as the most important medium for reaching millions. Scapegoating — blaming Jews, Communists, and the Weimar government for Germany’s problems gave people a clear enemy. Hitler’s image — carefully crafted as a strong, decisive leader who could save Germany.

The Role of the SA

The SA (Sturmabteilung), or Brownshirts, played a vital role in the Nazis’ rise. By 1932, the SA had over 400,000 members. They disrupted Communist and Social Democrat meetings, beat up political opponents, and protected Nazi rallies. The SA’s street violence gave many Germans the impression that the Weimar Republic was collapsing into chaos — and that only the Nazis could restore order. Ironically, the Nazis were creating much of that chaos themselves.

The Presidential Elections of 1932

In March 1932, Hitler stood against the ageing President Hindenburg in the presidential election. Hindenburg won with 53% of the vote, but Hitler gained an impressive 36.8% — over 13 million votes. This showed how far the Nazis had come from their dismal performance in the 1928 elections, when they won just 2.6% of the vote. Hitler was now a major national figure.

Key Fact

In the July 1932 Reichstag election, the Nazis became the largest party with 230 seats (37.3% of the vote). In November 1932, their support dipped slightly to 196 seats (33.1%), but they remained the biggest party in the Reichstag.

For example, the Wall Street Crash caused unemployment, which created fear of communism, which drove middle-class voters to the Nazis. This kind of linked analysis scores highly. Remember to include specific evidence — dates, statistics, and named individuals like Goebbels.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash of 1929 caused mass unemployment in Germany, destroying faith in the Weimar Republic and driving voters towards extremist parties like the Nazis and Communists.
  • Nazi support grew because Hitler offered something to every group, Goebbels ran brilliant propaganda campaigns, and the SA created chaos that made democracy look weak.
  • By July 1932, the Nazis were the largest party in the Reichstag with 230 seats — a dramatic rise from just 12 seats in 1928.

lessons.title: Hitler Becomes Chancellor 1932–33
lessons.description: The political scheming behind Hitler's appointment as Chancellor in January 1933.
lessons.content_html:
The Political Crisis of 1932

By late 1932, Germany’s democratic system was in crisis. The Reichstag was paralysed — no single party had a majority, and coalitions kept collapsing. President Hindenburg was ruling by emergency decree under Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution. Two Reichstag elections in 1932 (July and November) failed to produce a workable government. Voters were exhausted and disillusioned with democracy.

In the July 1932 election, the Nazis became the largest party with 230 seats (37.3% of the vote). Hitler demanded to be made Chancellor, but President Hindenburg refused. Hindenburg despised Hitler, calling him a “Bohemian corporal” and insisting he would never hand power to such a man.

Key Fact

Hitler did not seize power by force. He was appointed Chancellor through political scheming and backroom deals between Hindenburg, von Papen, and von Schleicher. Understanding this distinction is essential for the exam.

The Role of Franz von Papen

Franz von Papen had been Chancellor from June to November 1932. He was a wealthy, aristocratic politician who had very little support in the Reichstag — his government was nicknamed the “cabinet of barons.” When von Papen could not command a majority, Hindenburg replaced him with General Kurt von Schleicher in December 1932.

Von Papen was furious at being replaced and wanted revenge on von Schleicher. He began secret negotiations with Hitler, proposing a deal: Hitler would become Chancellor, and von Papen would become Vice-Chancellor. Von Papen believed he could control Hitler. He famously said, “Within two months we will have pushed Hitler so far into a corner that he’ll squeak.”

Von Papen’s plan was to surround Hitler with conservative ministers who would keep him in check. Only three of the twelve cabinet members would be Nazis. Von Papen assumed that Hitler, inexperienced in government, would be a puppet Chancellor while the conservatives pulled the strings behind the scenes. This proved to be one of the greatest miscalculations in modern history — within months, Hitler had dismantled democracy entirely.

The Fall of Von Schleicher

General Kurt von Schleicher lasted only 57 days as Chancellor. He tried to split the Nazi Party by offering the deputy leader, Gregor Strasser, a place in government. This failed. Von Schleicher then asked Hindenburg for the power to dissolve the Reichstag and rule by emergency decree, but Hindenburg refused — partly because von Papen had been whispering in his ear, telling him there was a better alternative.

Von Schleicher resigned on 28 January 1933. Hindenburg now faced a choice: either call yet another election (the fifth in a year, which would further destabilise Germany) or appoint a new Chancellor who might be able to command a Reichstag majority. Von Papen persuaded Hindenburg that a Hitler-led coalition was the safest option.

Hitler Appointed Chancellor — 30 January 1933

On 30 January 1933, President Hindenburg reluctantly appointed Adolf Hitler as Chancellor of Germany. The Nazi Party celebrated with a torchlight parade through the streets of Berlin. Hitler had achieved power not through a revolution or a military coup, but through the legal mechanisms of the Weimar Constitution — the very system he intended to destroy.

Key Fact

Hitler became Chancellor because of a combination of factors: the failure of other chancellors (Brüning, von Papen, von Schleicher), von Papen’s scheming and desire for revenge, Hindenburg’s exhaustion with political instability, and the Nazis’ status as the largest party in the Reichstag.

Hindenburg was 85 years old and increasingly frail. He had already refused Hitler once after the July 1932 election, but the political situation had only worsened. Von Schleicher’s failure left Hindenburg with few options. Von Papen convinced him that a coalition with only three Nazi cabinet members could be controlled. Hindenburg also feared that refusing Hitler again might provoke a Nazi uprising or civil war. Reluctantly, he agreed — a decision he would not live long enough to regret in full.

The November 1932 Election — A Warning Sign?

It is worth noting that in the November 1932 Reichstag election, Nazi support actually fell from 230 seats to 196 seats. The party was running out of money, and some voters were drifting back to other parties. Some historians argue that if Hindenburg had held out a little longer, the Nazi threat might have faded. Instead, the backroom deal between von Papen and Hitler gave the Nazis power at the very moment their electoral momentum was stalling.

lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on why Hitler became Chancellor, avoid the common mistake of simply listing reasons. Instead, show how the factors are connected. For example: “Von Papen’s desire for revenge on von Schleicher led him to approach Hitler, and Hindenburg agreed because von Schleicher had already failed.” This kind of linked reasoning is what moves you from Level 2 to Level 3 and beyond in “Explain Why” answers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 through political scheming, not a revolution — von Papen brokered the deal, believing he could control Hitler.
  • Hindenburg reluctantly agreed because all other options had failed — Brüning, von Papen, and von Schleicher had all been unable to form stable governments.
  • Nazi electoral support was actually declining by November 1932, making the timing of Hitler’s appointment all the more significant — he was given power just as his party’s momentum was fading.

lessons.title: Creating the Dictatorship: Reichstag Fire to Führer
lessons.description: How Hitler dismantled democracy in just 18 months, from the Reichstag Fire to becoming Führer.
lessons.content_html:
The Reichstag Fire — 27 February 1933

On the night of 27 February 1933, the Reichstag building was set ablaze. A young Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was found inside and arrested. Hitler immediately declared that the fire was evidence of a Communist plot to overthrow the government. He persuaded President Hindenburg to sign the Decree for the Protection of the People and the State (the Reichstag Fire Decree), which suspended key civil liberties — freedom of speech, freedom of the press, and the right to hold political meetings.

Key Fact

The Reichstag Fire Decree allowed the Nazis to arrest 4,000 Communist leaders in the days before the March 1933 election. With Communist opponents imprisoned and their meetings banned, the Nazis had a major advantage at the polls.

Historians still debate whether van der Lubbe acted alone or whether the Nazis started the fire themselves to create an excuse. Either way, Hitler exploited the crisis brilliantly. In the March 1933 election, the Nazis won 288 seats (43.9%) — still not a majority, but with the support of the nationalist DNVP, Hitler had enough votes to push through his next move.

The Enabling Act — 23 March 1933

The Enabling Act was the single most important step in Hitler’s destruction of democracy. It gave the Chancellor the power to pass laws without the Reichstag’s approval for four years. To pass the Act, Hitler needed a two-thirds majority in the Reichstag. He achieved this by:

  • Banning the 81 Communist deputies from attending (already arrested under the Reichstag Fire Decree).
  • Using the SA to intimidate remaining opponents — Brownshirts surrounded the opera house where the vote took place.
  • Promising the Centre Party that Catholic rights would be protected (a promise he later broke).

Only the Social Democrats (SPD) voted against it. Their leader, Otto Wels, made a courageous speech defending democracy, but it was too late. The Act passed 444 votes to 94.

Key Fact

The Enabling Act effectively made Hitler a legal dictator. He could now pass any law he wanted without parliamentary debate, without Hindenburg’s approval, and even laws that contradicted the Weimar Constitution.

Banning Other Parties and Trade Unions

With the Enabling Act in place, Hitler moved swiftly to eliminate all remaining opposition. In May 1933, trade unions were banned and their leaders arrested. Their offices were raided by the SA, and all workers were forced to join the new German Labour Front (DAF), controlled by the Nazis. This destroyed workers’ ability to strike or negotiate independently.

In July 1933, the Law Against the Formation of New Parties was passed, making the Nazi Party the only legal political party in Germany. The SPD was banned, and the remaining parties dissolved themselves under pressure. Germany was now a one-party state.

By mid-1933, opposition was extremely dangerous. The SA and the new secret police (Gestapo) arrested anyone who spoke out. Communist and SPD leaders were imprisoned in the first concentration camps at Dachau and elsewhere. The Centre Party dissolved itself after reaching a deal with Hitler (the Concordat with the Pope). Many Germans were willing to accept the end of democracy in exchange for the promise of stability and economic recovery after the chaos of the Weimar years.

The Night of the Long Knives — 30 June 1934

By 1934, the biggest threat to Hitler came not from the opposition, but from within the Nazi Party itself. Ernst Röhm, the leader of the SA, commanded over 3 million Brownshirts and wanted a “second revolution” — he believed the SA should absorb the regular army and that the Nazi revolution should go further, redistributing wealth from the rich. This alarmed Hitler for several reasons:

  • The German army would never accept being merged with the undisciplined SA. Hitler needed the army’s support.
  • Industrialists who funded the Nazis feared Röhm’s socialist ideas.
  • Himmler and Göring were jealous of Röhm’s power and fed Hitler intelligence (some possibly fabricated) that Röhm was planning a coup.

On the night of 30 June 1934, the SS arrested and executed Röhm and at least 85 other SA leaders. The purge also targeted non-Nazis whom Hitler wanted removed, including former Chancellor von Schleicher (shot dead along with his wife). The event became known as the Night of the Long Knives.

The purge had three major consequences. First, it removed the SA as a rival power base — the SA was reduced to a minor organisation, and the SS under Heinrich Himmler became the dominant force. Second, it won over the army, which was relieved that the SA had been neutralised. Third, it showed that Hitler was willing to use murder to maintain power, sending a terrifying message to anyone who might oppose him. A new law retrospectively legalised the killings as “emergency measures.”

Death of Hindenburg — Hitler Becomes Führer

On 2 August 1934, President Hindenburg died at the age of 86. Within hours, Hitler merged the offices of President and Chancellor, declaring himself Führer (leader) of Germany. There would be no new presidential election. The German army immediately swore a personal oath of allegiance — not to Germany, not to the constitution, but to Adolf Hitler personally. This bound every soldier to obey Hitler, regardless of orders.

Key Fact

By August 1934, Hitler had complete control of Germany. He was head of state, head of government, head of the armed forces, and leader of the only legal political party. The Weimar Republic was dead.

lessons.exam_tip_html: This topic is packed with key events. For “Explain Why” questions, you need to identify specific events (Reichstag Fire, Enabling Act, Night of the Long Knives) and explain their significance — how each one moved Hitler closer to total power. For “How Useful” source questions, always consider the context — what was happening politically when the source was created, and how this affects its reliability and usefulness.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Reichstag Fire gave Hitler the excuse to suspend civil liberties and arrest Communist opponents, while the Enabling Act made him a legal dictator who could pass laws without parliament.
  • The Night of the Long Knives removed the SA as a rival, won the army’s loyalty, and showed Hitler would use murder to maintain power.
  • By August 1934 — just 18 months after becoming Chancellor — Hitler had combined the offices of President and Chancellor, banned all other parties, and secured a personal oath of allegiance from the army.

lessons.title: The Nazi Police State, Propaganda & Opposition
lessons.description: How the Nazis controlled Germany through terror, propaganda, and the suppression of opposition.
lessons.content_html:
The Police State: Terror and Control

Once Hitler had established the dictatorship, the Nazi regime maintained power through a combination of terror and propaganda. The police state ensured that opposition was crushed, while Goebbels’ propaganda machine controlled what people saw, heard, and believed.

The Gestapo

The Gestapo (Geheime Staatspolizei) was the Nazi secret police, established in 1933 and later placed under Heinrich Himmler’s control. The Gestapo could arrest anyone suspected of opposing the regime and hold them without trial. They operated outside the normal legal system — there was no appeal and no court hearing. Much of the Gestapo’s effectiveness came from ordinary Germans who informed on their neighbours, colleagues, and even family members. Fear of being reported made people censor themselves.

Key Fact

The Gestapo had around 32,000 officers for a country of 66 million people. Their real power lay not in their numbers but in the climate of fear they created — anyone could be an informer.

The SS and Concentration Camps

The SS (Schutzstaffel) began as Hitler’s personal bodyguard but grew under Himmler into the most powerful organisation in the Third Reich. By 1936, the SS controlled all police and security forces in Germany. SS members were fanatically loyal to Hitler and were trained to be ruthless.

Concentration camps were set up from March 1933, with Dachau being the first. Initially, they held political prisoners — Communists, Social Democrats, trade unionists, and anyone who criticised the regime. Conditions were brutal: prisoners were beaten, starved, and forced into hard labour. The existence of the camps served as a warning to the entire population about the consequences of opposition.

Control of the Legal System

The Nazis also controlled the courts. Judges were expected to make decisions that supported the Nazi state. A new People’s Court was established in 1934 to try cases of treason — its judges were hand-picked Nazis, and defendants had no right to appeal. The number of offences carrying the death penalty rose from 3 in 1933 to 46 by 1943.

Under the Weimar Republic, Germany had an independent judiciary that protected individual rights. The Nazis destroyed this independence. Judges who did not support the regime were sacked. Laws were changed to make political opposition a criminal offence. Defence lawyers in political cases were often intimidated. The legal system became a tool of Nazi control rather than a protector of citizens’ rights.

Goebbels and the Ministry of Propaganda

In March 1933, Hitler appointed Joseph Goebbels as head of the new Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. Goebbels controlled all forms of communication and culture in Germany. His aim was simple: to ensure that every German heard only the Nazi message.

Censorship was total. All newspapers were either shut down or brought under Nazi control. Editors were told what they could and could not print. Books by Jewish, Communist, and liberal authors were publicly burned in May 1933 — over 25,000 books were destroyed in Berlin alone. Radio stations broadcast only approved content, and Goebbels ensured cheap “People’s Receivers” were produced so that every household could hear Nazi broadcasts.

Key Fact

By 1939, 70% of German households owned a radio — the highest proportion in the world. Loudspeakers were placed in cafés, factories, and public squares so that even those without radios could hear Hitler’s speeches and Nazi broadcasts.

Rallies, Sport, and the Berlin Olympics (1936)

The Nuremberg Rallies, held annually, were massive displays of Nazi power. Hundreds of thousands attended, with marching columns, searchlights, flags, and speeches from Hitler that lasted hours. The rallies were filmed by Leni Riefenstahl, whose documentary Triumph of the Will (1935) became one of the most famous propaganda films ever made.

The 1936 Berlin Olympics were used to showcase Nazi Germany to the world. The Nazis temporarily removed anti-Jewish signs, presented a clean and efficient image, and Germany topped the medal table with 89 medals. However, the African-American athlete Jesse Owens won four gold medals, undermining Nazi claims of Aryan racial superiority. Despite this, the Olympics were largely seen as a propaganda triumph for the regime.

Control of Culture and the Arts

The Nazis controlled art, architecture, literature, and film. Modern art was condemned as “degenerate” and replaced with paintings glorifying the Aryan ideal — healthy peasants, muscular soldiers, and idealised German landscapes. Architecture became monumental, with Albert Speer designing grandiose buildings to demonstrate Nazi power. Films promoted Nazi ideology, and all scripts had to be approved by the propaganda ministry.

Attempts to Control the Churches

Germany was roughly two-thirds Protestant and one-third Catholic. The Nazis wanted to control the Churches because they were the only organisations with the loyalty and reach to potentially challenge the regime.

In July 1933, Hitler signed the Concordat with the Pope. The Catholic Church agreed not to interfere in German politics, and in return Hitler promised to leave Catholic schools, youth groups, and organisations alone. Hitler broke this promise almost immediately, closing Catholic youth groups and arresting priests who spoke out.

For Protestants, the Nazis created the Reich Church in 1933, led by Ludwig Müller. The Reich Church promoted Nazi ideology, displayed swastikas alongside crosses, and tried to merge Christianity with Nazism. Many Protestants rejected this.

Pastor Martin Niemöller was a Protestant pastor who initially supported the Nazis but turned against the regime when he saw the Reich Church distorting Christianity. In 1934, he helped form the Confessing Church, which rejected Nazi interference in religion. Niemöller was arrested in 1937 and spent the rest of the Nazi era in concentration camps at Sachsenhausen and Dachau. His famous post-war quote — “First they came for the Communists, and I did not speak out…” — became a powerful warning about the dangers of political silence.

Youth Opposition

Not all young people accepted Nazi control. The Edelweiss Pirates were groups of young working-class Germans who refused to join the Hitler Youth. They wore distinctive badges, went on hiking trips away from Nazi supervision, sang anti-Nazi songs, and sometimes attacked Hitler Youth patrols. In Cologne in 1944, twelve Edelweiss Pirates were publicly hanged.

The Swing Youth were middle-class teenagers who rejected Nazi culture by listening to banned American jazz and swing music, dancing in clubs, and adopting non-conformist fashion. They deliberately socialised with Jewish people and rejected the militarism of the Hitler Youth. The Gestapo raided swing clubs, and some Swing Youth members were sent to concentration camps.

Opposition to the Nazis was brave but ultimately limited in its impact. The Gestapo, SS, and concentration camps made organised resistance extremely dangerous. The Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth were annoying to the regime but did not threaten its survival. Church leaders like Niemöller were isolated and imprisoned. Most Germans either supported the regime, kept quiet out of fear, or felt powerless to act. The police state was highly effective at preventing any serious challenge to Nazi rule.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers both control methods (terror + propaganda) and opposition. For “How Far Do You Agree” interpretation questions, you might be asked whether the Nazis maintained power mainly through fear or mainly through consent. Always discuss both sides and reach a balanced judgement. Use specific examples: Gestapo informers for fear, cheap radios for propaganda, Edelweiss Pirates for opposition.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Nazi police state used the Gestapo, SS, and concentration camps to crush opposition, while controlling the legal system to ensure courts served the regime.
  • Goebbels’ propaganda machine controlled all media, culture, and public events — from censored newspapers and cheap radios to the Nuremberg Rallies and the 1936 Berlin Olympics.
  • Opposition existed (Niemöller, Edelweiss Pirates, Swing Youth) but was limited in its effectiveness because the police state made organised resistance extremely dangerous.

lessons.title: Life in Nazi Germany: Women, Youth & Persecution
lessons.description: Nazi policies on women, young people, workers, and the escalating persecution of minorities.
lessons.content_html:
Nazi Views on Women

The Nazis had a clear ideology about women’s role in society. They believed women should focus on the “three Ks” — Kinder, Küche, Kirche (Children, Kitchen, Church). Women were expected to be wives and mothers, not workers or professionals. This was a deliberate reversal of the freedoms women had gained during the Weimar Republic, when women had voted, entered professions, and enjoyed greater social independence.

Key Fact

The Nazis introduced marriage loans of 1,000 marks for couples where the wife gave up work. For each child born, a quarter of the loan was written off. Women who had four or more children received the Motherhood Cross (bronze for 4, silver for 6, gold for 8 children).

Employment: Women were discouraged from working in professions. Female doctors, lawyers, and civil servants were dismissed. Women were encouraged to leave their jobs and return home. However, by the late 1930s, as rearmament created labour shortages, the Nazis quietly reversed this policy and encouraged women back into the workforce.

Appearance: The ideal Nazi woman wore no make-up, did not smoke, wore flat shoes, and had her hair in a bun or plaits. Trousers, high heels, hair dye, and slimming diets were all frowned upon. The ideal Nazi woman was healthy, natural, and devoted to producing children for the Fatherland.

The birth rate did increase — from 15.1 per thousand in 1933 to 20.4 per thousand in 1939. Marriage loans and the Motherhood Cross appeared to have some effect. However, the policies were not entirely successful. Many women resented losing their jobs and independence. By 1939, there were actually more women in employment than in 1933, because rearmament created such a demand for workers that the Nazis had to abandon their own ideology. The contradiction between Nazi ideals and economic reality was never resolved.

Hitler Youth and the League of German Maidens

The Nazis aimed to control young people from an early age. The Hitler Youth (Hitlerjugend) was the main organisation for boys aged 14–18, while the League of German Maidens (Bund Deutscher Mädel, or BDM) was for girls of the same age. Younger children joined the German Young People (ages 10–14) or the Young Girls (ages 10–14).

Membership of the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1936. By 1939, over 8 million young Germans were members. Boys were trained in physical fitness, camping, map-reading, and military skills. They were also indoctrinated with Nazi ideology — loyalty to Hitler, racial superiority, and anti-Semitism. Girls in the BDM learned domestic skills, childcare, and fitness, preparing them for their future role as mothers.

Education Under the Nazis

Schools were transformed to serve the Nazi state. The curriculum was rewritten: history lessons glorified Germany’s past and blamed the Jews for Germany’s problems; biology taught racial theory and the superiority of the “Aryan race”; physical education was increased to five periods per week to prepare boys for military service; and girls focused on domestic science.

Teachers were required to join the National Socialist Teachers’ League. Those who refused were sacked. Teachers attended training camps where they learned how to teach the Nazi curriculum. Jewish teachers were dismissed. Textbooks were rewritten to include Nazi propaganda — even maths problems involved calculating the cost of keeping disabled people in institutions.

Nazi textbooks included questions like: “A mentally ill person costs the state 4 marks a day. There are 300,000 mentally ill people in care. How much do they cost the state annually?” These questions were designed to make students accept that disabled people were a burden on society, preparing public opinion for the later euthanasia programme. This is a chilling example of how education was used as a tool of indoctrination.

Reducing Unemployment

One of the Nazis’ most popular policies was their apparent success in reducing unemployment. Official figures showed unemployment falling from over 6 million in 1933 to under 500,000 by 1938. However, the reality was more complicated.

Key Fact

Nazi unemployment figures were misleading. Invisible unemployment meant that Jews, women who left work, and men in the National Labour Service (RAD) were not counted. If these groups had been included, the real figure would have been significantly higher.

The main methods used to reduce unemployment were:

  • National Labour Service (RAD) — all men aged 18–25 had to do six months of manual labour, such as building autobahns, planting forests, and draining marshes. Pay was low, and conditions were harsh.
  • Autobahns — a massive motorway-building programme that employed 125,000 workers. The autobahns also served military purposes, allowing rapid troop movements.
  • Rearmament — from 1935, Hitler openly rearmed Germany in defiance of the Treaty of Versailles. Weapons factories, shipyards, and the new Luftwaffe (air force) created millions of jobs.
  • Conscription — introduced in 1935, military service removed hundreds of thousands of young men from the unemployment register.

The German Labour Front and Strength Through Joy

After banning trade unions, the Nazis created the German Labour Front (DAF), led by Robert Ley. Workers could not strike or negotiate wages, but the DAF ran two schemes to keep them content:

Strength Through Joy (KdF) organised leisure activities for workers — subsidised holidays, theatre trips, sporting events, and even cruises. The most famous KdF project was the Volkswagen (“People’s Car”), which workers could save towards. However, not a single Volkswagen was ever delivered to a civilian — the factory switched to military production when war broke out. Beauty of Labour improved working conditions by installing better lighting, canteens, and washing facilities in factories.

The Persecution of Minorities

Nazi racial ideology placed the “Aryan race” at the top of a racial hierarchy. Groups deemed racially “inferior” or socially “undesirable” faced systematic persecution:

  • Slavs — considered racially inferior; millions would later be murdered or enslaved during the war.
  • Roma and Sinti — classified as “asocials” and subjected to forced sterilisation, deportation, and later genocide.
  • Homosexuals — at least 10,000 men were sent to concentration camps. Gay men were forced to wear pink triangles.
  • People with disabilities — seen as a burden on the state. From 1934, over 350,000 were forcibly sterilised under the Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring.

The Persecution of Jewish People

Anti-Semitism was at the core of Nazi ideology. The persecution of Jewish people escalated throughout the 1930s:

April 1933

Boycott of Jewish Shops

SA members stood outside Jewish-owned businesses, warning people not to enter. The boycott lasted one day officially, but harassment continued.

1933–34

Professional Exclusion

Jewish people were banned from the civil service, teaching, journalism, and other professions.

September 1935

Nuremberg Laws

The Nuremberg Laws stripped Jewish people of German citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jewish Germans. Jewish people were no longer citizens — they were “subjects.”

9–10 November 1938

Kristallnacht (“Night of Broken Glass”)

Kristallnacht saw the destruction of over 1,000 synagogues, 7,500 Jewish businesses, and the arrest of around 30,000 Jewish men who were sent to concentration camps. At least 91 Jewish people were killed. The Jewish community was then fined 1 billion marks for the damage.

Key Fact

The persecution of Jewish people escalated from social exclusion (boycotts, 1933) to legal discrimination (Nuremberg Laws, 1935) to organised violence (Kristallnacht, 1938). After Kristallnacht, around 250,000 Jewish people fled Germany — those who remained faced even worse treatment during the war.

Several factors explain why most Germans did not oppose the persecution of Jewish people. Anti-Semitism had deep roots in European culture and was not unique to the Nazis. Nazi propaganda blamed Jews for Germany’s economic problems, reinforcing existing prejudices. The police state made any form of protest extremely dangerous — helping Jewish people could result in imprisonment or death. Some Germans benefited directly from persecution, buying Jewish property or taking over Jewish businesses at below-market prices. Others simply looked away, telling themselves it was not their concern.

Read the question carefully to identify which area is being assessed. For “How Far Do You Agree” questions about whether the Nazis improved life for Germans, always consider who benefited and who suffered — the answer depends entirely on which group you are discussing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Nazis pushed women back into traditional roles (Kinder, Küche, Kirche) with marriage loans and the Motherhood Cross, but had to reverse course when rearmament created labour shortages.
  • Young people were indoctrinated through the Hitler Youth, the BDM, and a rewritten school curriculum that promoted racial theory and military values.
  • Unemployment fell dramatically, but the figures were misleading due to invisible unemployment, and workers lost the right to strike or negotiate wages.
  • The persecution of minorities — especially Jewish people — escalated from boycotts (1933) to the Nuremberg Laws (1935) to the organised violence of Kristallnacht (1938).

The 'Night of Broken Glass' (9–10 November 1938), a coordinated attack on Jewish synagogues, homes, and businesses across Germany. Over 1,000 synagogues were burned, 7,500 businesses destroyed, and around 30,000 Jewish men were arrested.
